title: Stand on the rock
sum: Ignatius greets 'Polycarp, overseer of the church of the Smyrnaeans, or rather, one overseen by God' (1:0). He praises Polycarp's mind, 'firmly settled as on an immovable rock', and is glad to have seen his face (1:1). Then comes a stream of short commands: run your race harder, 'Do justice to your place', care for union, 'Carry everyone, as the Lord carries you', 'Put up with everyone in love', pray without a break, speak to people one by one, 'Carry everyone's diseases, as a perfect athlete' (1:2-3).

views.H: Lightfoot: 'Like the Pastoral Epistles of S. Paul, with which it has many points in common, this letter is the exhortation of an older servant of Christ to a younger friend who holds a responsible office in the Church.' He and Pearson read 1:1 as showing Ignatius first met Polycarp at Smyrna.
views.N: The house on the rock (Matthew 7:24-25), 'Put up with one another in love' (Ephesians 4:2, Lake's margin), and 'carried our diseases' (Matthew 8:17, Lake's margin) are woven into the commands.
views.C: The overseer's duties here are pastoral: prayer, patience, care for each person. On the office itself, see the cards at 1 Timothy 3 and Acts 20:28.

echoes: Matthew 7:24-25; Ephesians 4:2; Galatians 6:2; Matthew 8:17; Isaiah 53:4; 1 Thessalonians 5:17; 2 Timothy 4:7

settings.by: Ignatius, overseer of the church at Antioch in Syria, a prisoner under guard on his way to Rome
settings.to: Polycarp, overseer of the church at Smyrna, who had received Ignatius during his stay there
settings.when: At Troas, about to sail suddenly for Neapolis (8:1; Eusebius, Church History 3.36.10)
settings.why: To greet Polycarp and, by the play on 'overseer', to remind him that his oversight answers to God's.
settings.readers: Polycarp, named in the greeting; the church at Smyrna heard its overseer greeted, since the letter turns to it at 6:1

settings.by: Ignatius, overseer of the church at Antioch in Syria, a prisoner under guard on his way to Rome
settings.to: Polycarp, overseer of the church at Smyrna, who had received Ignatius during his stay there
settings.when: At Troas, about to sail suddenly for Neapolis (8:1; Eusebius, Church History 3.36.10)
settings.why: To encourage a church leader under pressure and to set out his duties: patience with all, prayer, care for each person, gentleness with the troublesome, firmness against false teachers.
settings.readers: Polycarp in the first place; Lightfoot notes the counsel was 'not private' and was meant for the church as well

title: Not every wound
sum: Loving good disciples earns no thanks; the skill is to win 'the more troublesome ones' with gentleness. 'The same plaster does not heal every wound' (2:1). Polycarp must be 'sharp like the snake' and 'pure like the dove', using his flesh for what he can see and prayer for what he cannot (2:2). 'The time demands you', as pilots need winds and a storm-tossed sailor a harbor. 'Keep a clear head, as God's athlete. The prize is incorruption and eternal life' (2:3).

views.H: Lake on 2:3: 'the details are hopelessly obscure. Possibly something has dropped out of the text'; the 'prize' is a 'money-prize' of the Greek games.
views.N: Matthew 10:16 (Lake's margin), in the singular; Luke 6:32 and Matthew 5:46 behind 'that earns you no thanks'; Paul's crown of the games (1 Corinthians 9:24-25).
views.C: The overseer as a doctor who fits the remedy to the patient: a picture of pastoral care that varies with the person.

echoes: Matthew 10:16; Luke 6:32; Matthew 5:46-48; 1 Corinthians 9:24-25; Ignatius to the Ephesians 7:2

title: Like a struck anvil
sum: Polycarp must not be shaken by those 'who seem trustworthy but teach something different': 'Stand firm like a struck anvil. A great athlete takes the blows and wins' (3:1). He must wait for 'the one who is above time: the timeless, the invisible, visible for our sake; the untouchable, beyond suffering, able to suffer for our sake; who endured in every way for our sake' (3:2).

views.H: Lightfoot: this is the only place the letter touches the heresy of the companion letter to Smyrna, and so it 'escaped with comparatively few changes' from the interpolator of the long recension.
views.N: 'Teach something different' is the verb of 1 Timothy 1:3 and 6:3. The titles of 3:2 can be read beside John 1:14 and 1 John 1:1, the Word who became flesh and whom 'our hands touched'.
views.C: The titles of 3:2 are close to the 'one doctor' of Ignatius to the Ephesians 7:2: one who is beyond time and suffering, yet truly suffered.

deep.b:
Ignatius builds 3:2 as a ladder of opposites. The one 'above time' is 'timeless' (achronos); the 'invisible' (aoratos) is 'visible for our sake'; the 'untouchable' (apsēlaphētos) and 'beyond suffering' (apathēs) is 'able to suffer for our sake' (pathētos); and he 'endured in every way for our sake'. Lightfoot points out that no clause balances 'untouchable', and that the evidence 'forbids the insertion' of one. The same pair, 'first able to suffer and then beyond suffering', ends the hymn of Ignatius to the Ephesians 7:2.

Those 'who seem trustworthy but teach something different' (3:1) are not named. Lightfoot finds in this chapter 'a passing allusion expressed in general terms' to the heresy of the companion letter to Smyrna, whose teachers said Christ suffered only in appearance (Ignatius to the Smyrnaeans 2:1); read that way, the titles answer them: the one beyond suffering truly suffered 'for our sake'. Read beside John 1:14 and 1 John 1:1, the 'untouchable' is the word of life 'our hands touched'. See the topics on the Incarnation and on docetism.

echoes: 1 Timothy 1:3; 1 Timothy 6:3; John 1:14; 1 John 1:1; Colossians 1:15; Ignatius to the Ephesians 7:2; Ignatius to the Smyrnaeans 2:1

title: Widows and slaves
sum: 'The widows must not be neglected. After the Lord, you must be the one who cares for them.' Nothing should be done without Polycarp's approval, and he nothing without God (4:1). Gatherings should be more frequent; he should seek out everyone by name (4:2). He must not look down on slaves, but they must not be puffed up; they should not long to be set free 'from the common fund, so that they are not found to be slaves of desire' (4:3).

views.H: Lightfoot reads the verse as assuming a church fund that could buy slaves their freedom: since the money was limited, 'it was necessary to select cases of special hardship'.
views.N: Widows: Acts 6:1; 1 Timothy 5:3-16; James 1:27. Slaves: 1 Corinthians 7:21-23; 1 Timothy 6:1-2 (Lake's margin); Ephesians 6:5-9; Philemon.
views.C: The overseer personally oversees the care of widows and the gatherings of the church. On slavery, see the cards at Ephesians 6 and Philemon.

deep.h: What 4:3 does and does not say
deep.b:
The Greek has three parts. First, a word to the overseer: 'Do not look down on male and female slaves' (doulous kai doulas mē hyperēphanei). Second, a word about the slaves: they must not be 'puffed up', but should serve 'all the more' for God's glory, 'so that from God they may gain a better freedom'. Third: 'They should not long to be set free from the common fund (apo tou koinou), so that they are not found to be slaves of desire.'

The verse does not forbid freeing slaves, or freedom gained another way; it warns slaves against setting their hearts on being freed at the common cost, and it names a worse slavery, to desire. Lightfoot reads to koinon as 'the common fund, the public money', points to the Apostolic Constitutions (4.9), where the church's money is directed to freeing slaves, and explains the warning by the size of the fund. He reports that Zahn took the words as 'the community', and rejects that: with this verb 'we should certainly expect hypo tou koinou, not apo tou koinou, in this sense'.

Lightfoot hears 1 Timothy 6:2 in 'serve all the more' (slaves with believing masters 'should serve them better still'), and 1 Corinthians 7:21 'according to one, though not the most probable, interpretation', the one in which Paul tells the slave to make use of his slavery. The site's 1 Corinthians 7:21 follows the other reading, 'if you are able to become free, make use of it instead', and its note sets out both; 7:22 calls the called slave 'the Lord's freed person'.

This page gives Lightfoot's reading of the verse, the one opened for it. On how churches today read the Bible's words on slavery, see the cards at Ephesians 6 and Philemon.

echoes: Acts 6:1; 1 Timothy 5:3-16; James 1:27; James 2:2; 1 Corinthians 7:21-23; 1 Timothy 6:1-2; Philemon 1:16

settings.by: Ignatius, overseer of the church at Antioch in Syria, a prisoner under guard on his way to Rome
settings.to: Polycarp, overseer of the church at Smyrna, who had received Ignatius during his stay there
settings.when: At Troas, about to sail suddenly for Neapolis (8:1; Eusebius, Church History 3.36.10)
settings.why: To make the overseer himself the guardian of the widows, to have the church meet more often, and to set the place of slaves in the church: not despised, not proud, not longing to be freed at the common cost.
settings.readers: Polycarp, who was to carry this out; the widows in the church's care (4:1); every member, sought out 'by name' (4:2); and the male and female slaves among the believers (4:3)

title: Husbands, wives and the single life
sum: Polycarp must run from 'the evil arts' and preach against them. Wives are to love the Lord and be content with their husbands; husbands are to 'love their wives as the Lord loves the church' (5:1). Anyone who can remain unmarried 'in purity for the honor of the Lord's flesh' should do so without boasting: 'Should he boast, he is lost; and if it becomes known beyond the overseer, he is ruined.' 'Men and women who marry should make their union with the overseer's approval, so that the marriage may follow the Lord and not desire' (5:2).
readings: Read as the overseer's approval 'in the Lord' (Lightfoot)

Lightfoot paraphrases: 'Let those who marry seek the approval of the bishop for their union', and connects it with Paul's 'only in the Lord' (1 Corinthians 7:39): the overseer's approval is to see that the marriage 'may follow the Lord and not desire'.
Read as a witness to the religious character of marriage (the Catholic Encyclopedia)
The Catholic Encyclopedia (1910), a reference work rather than a church document, lists the chapter as a witness to 'the religious character of matrimony'.

views.H: Lightfoot: there is 'no indication here of an "order" of virgins'; the one who stays single tells the overseer and no one else, which 'contrasts with the usage of a later age, where the public profession of such vows was an essential feature'.
views.N: Ephesians 5:25-29 (Lake's margin) for husbands; 1 Corinthians 7 for the single life and marriage 'only in the Lord' (1 Corinthians 7:39); 1 Corinthians 6:15-20 for 'the Lord's flesh'.
views.C: On the single life and vows, see the cards at 1 Corinthians 7 and Matthew 19:12; on marriage as a sacrament, the card at Ephesians 5:32. The verse asks for the overseer's approval; it does not say who performs a wedding.

deep.b:
'If anyone is able to remain in purity for the honor of the Lord's flesh, let him remain so without boasting.' Hagneia, 'purity', is here staying unmarried and chaste. The reason given is 'the honor of the Lord's flesh': Lightfoot explains it from 1 Corinthians 6:15, where believers' bodies are members of Christ. The warning is sharp: the one who boasts 'is lost', and 'if it becomes known beyond the overseer, he is ruined' (ephthartai, 'is corrupted'). Lightfoot takes this as the person's purpose of chastity, known to the overseer but kept from public praise; he rejects the rendering 'if he be better known than the bishop'. The Greek manuscripts differ on the word behind 'beyond' (see the variants), but Lightfoot takes both readings to mean the same: known to no one but the overseer.

Paul honored the single life as a gift and refused to make it a rule (1 Corinthians 7:7, 35). Ignatius likewise honors it but guards it against pride.

'Men and women who marry should make their union with the overseer's approval (meta gnōmēs tou episkopou), so that the marriage may follow the Lord and not desire.' Gnōmē is the same word as 'approval' in 4:1 ('Let nothing be done without your approval'); Lake translates 'consent'. Lightfoot thinks of Paul's 'only in the Lord' (1 Corinthians 7:39) and points to later writers on 'the sanction given by the Church to marriages in the early ages'. Lightfoot also suggests that the word for husband and wife, symbios, 'life-partner', may have been chosen because it covered the unions of slaves, which Roman law did not count as marriage.

Ignatius does not describe a wedding service, who leads it, or what happens if the overseer withholds approval. The site has not opened the churches' own rules on who must approve or witness a marriage, and does not state them here; the cards on marriage at Ephesians 5:32, 2 Corinthians 6 and Matthew 19 set out related questions.

echoes: Ephesians 5:25-29; 1 Corinthians 7:7-8; 1 Corinthians 7:32-39; 1 Corinthians 6:15-20; Matthew 19:12; Hebrews 13:4

settings.what: Husbands, wives and the single life
settings.by: Ignatius, overseer of the church at Antioch in Syria, a prisoner under guard on his way to Rome
settings.to: Polycarp, overseer of the church at Smyrna, who had received Ignatius during his stay there
settings.when: At Troas, about to sail suddenly for Neapolis (8:1; Eusebius, Church History 3.36.10)
settings.why: To have Polycarp preach against the evil arts and guide the married and the unmarried: love and contentment in marriage, humility in the single life, and the overseer's knowledge of both choices.
settings.readers: Polycarp, who is to speak to 'my sisters' and charge 'my brothers' (5:1); the wives and husbands of the church; those who stayed single 'in purity' (5:2); and those about to marry (5:2)

title: God's soldiers
sum: Now Ignatius speaks to the whole church: 'Pay attention to the overseer, so that God may pay attention to you.' He offers himself as 'a life in exchange' for those who submit to the overseer, the elders and the deacons. 'Toil together with one another, compete together, run together, suffer together, rest together, rise together' (6:1). Then the army: please your commander, do not desert; 'Let your baptism remain as your weapons, your faith as a helmet, your love as a spear, your endurance as full armor'; let your deeds be 'your deposits', so that you receive 'the back pay you have earned' (6:2).

views.H: Ignatius borrows three Latin army words (deserter, deposits, back pay). Lake explains the soldiers' savings bank; Lightfoot that from a prisoner chained to soldiers 'nothing else was to be expected'.
views.N: Ephesians 6:13-17 and 1 Thessalonians 5:8 (the armor), 2 Timothy 2:3-4 (Lake's margin: pleasing the one who enlisted you), 1 Corinthians 9:7 (a soldier's pay), 1 Corinthians 4:1 (stewards and assistants).
views.C: The whole church, not only its ministers, is 'God's stewards ... and his assistants' (Lightfoot against Pearson). The order overseer, elders, deacons is that of all the letters; see the cards at 1 Timothy 3 and Philippians 1:1.

deep.b:
Ignatius builds the picture from the Roman army he knew from his guards. Pay (opsōnia) came from the commander; a 'deserter' (desertōr) lost everything. Lake's footnote: 'It was the custom in the Roman army to pay to the soldiers only the half of any gratuities allowed them. The other half was "deposited" in a regimental savings bank, and was paid out to each soldier, when, and if, he was honourably discharged from the service.' The Latin deposita are those savings, and accepta the sums paid out. Lightfoot quotes Vegetius: the soldier who knows his savings are with the standards never thinks of deserting.

So the Christian's good deeds are banked with God and paid out at the end; to desert is to lose them. Baptism is the soldier's arms (Lightfoot: his 'shield'), faith the helmet, love the spear, endurance the full armor. Paul's armor in Ephesians 6:13-17 assigns the pieces differently, and his 'all of God's armor' is the same word as 'full armor' here.

echoes: Ephesians 6:11-17; 1 Thessalonians 5:8; 2 Timothy 2:3-4; 1 Corinthians 9:7; 1 Corinthians 4:1; 1 Peter 4:10; Hebrews 13:17

settings.by: Ignatius, overseer of the church at Antioch in Syria, a prisoner under guard on his way to Rome
settings.to: The church at Smyrna, addressed directly (the Greek 'you' is plural)
settings.when: At Troas, about to sail suddenly for Neapolis (8:1; Eusebius, Church History 3.36.10)
settings.why: To bind the Smyrnaean church to its overseer and to one another, and to keep it steady under pressure, as soldiers who will be paid at the end.
settings.readers: The Christians of Smyrna, hearing the letter read; Lightfoot thinks Polycarp counted it among 'the letters of Ignatius, the ones he sent us' (Polycarp to the Philippians 13:2)

title: God's runner for Syria
sum: The church at Antioch is at peace, and Ignatius is 'more cheerful', if only through suffering he may reach God (7:1). Polycarp should call 'a council most fit for God' and elect someone dear and tireless, 'who can be called God's runner', to go to Syria (7:2). 'No Christian has authority over himself: he spends his time on God' (7:3).

views.H: Polycarp's own letter shows he expected to send an envoy: 'If anyone goes to Syria, he should carry the letter from you as well. I will do this if I get a good opportunity, either myself or someone I send as an envoy' (Polycarp to the Philippians 13:1). Lightfoot: Polycarp 'refers to this intended delegate'.
views.N: The church elects (Acts 14:23; 2 Corinthians 8:19); 'Christian' is the name first given at Antioch (Acts 11:26).
views.C: The overseer calls the council and the church elects; see the card at Acts 14:23 on who chooses ministers.

echoes: Acts 11:26; Acts 14:23; 2 Corinthians 8:19; Polycarp to the Philippians 13:1; Ignatius to the Philadelphians 10:1; Ignatius to the Smyrnaeans 11:2

settings.what: The envoy to Syria, and letters to the churches ahead
settings.by: Ignatius, overseer of the church at Antioch in Syria, a prisoner under guard on his way to Rome
settings.to: Polycarp, and through him the church at Smyrna (the 'you' moves between singular and plural)
settings.when: At Troas, about to sail suddenly for Neapolis (8:1; Eusebius, Church History 3.36.10)
settings.why: To have Polycarp organize the churches of Asia to send envoys and letters to Antioch, since Ignatius's sudden departure kept him from writing to them himself.
settings.readers: Polycarp (named at 7:2 and 8:2) and the Smyrnaean church, which was to hold the council and send 'God's runner'

title: Write to the churches ahead
sum: Because his guards are sailing suddenly 'from Troas to Neapolis', Ignatius cannot write to all the churches. Polycarp must write to 'the churches ahead', so that they too send messengers or letters (8:1). Ignatius greets everyone by name, 'the wife of the procurator' with her household, Attalus, and the one to be sent to Syria, 'and Polycarp who sends him' (8:2). He prays they remain 'in the unity and the oversight of God', and greets Alce, 'a name dear to me' (8:3).

views.H: Neapolis was 'The port-town of Philippi' (Lightfoot), 'The modern Cavalla' (Lake). Lake on 8:1: 'The combination of singular and plural is very strange'. The Catholic Encyclopedia (1910): 'the altered plans of his guards, necessitating a hurried departure from Troas,' left the task to Polycarp.
views.N: Paul's crossing from Troas to Neapolis (Acts 16:11) and his greetings by name (Romans 16).
views.C: One overseer asked to write to other churches on behalf of another: the churches of the second century kept in touch by letters and envoys.

echoes: Acts 16:11-12; Acts 20:5-6; Polycarp to the Philippians 13:1-2; Ignatius to the Smyrnaeans 13:2; Martyrdom of Polycarp 17:2; Romans 16:1-16

settings.by: Ignatius, overseer of the church at Antioch in Syria, a prisoner under guard on his way to Rome
settings.to: The church at Smyrna, through Polycarp: everyone by name, and named households and friends
settings.when: At Troas, about to sail suddenly for Neapolis (8:1; Eusebius, Church History 3.36.10)
settings.why: To greet the people Ignatius had come to know at Smyrna, and to commend the one who would go to Syria and Polycarp who sends him.
settings.readers: The household of 'the wife of the procurator', with her children; Attalus; the one to be sent to Syria; Polycarp; and Alce, also greeted in Ignatius to the Smyrnaeans 13:2
